sentences.text: At 9:00 that night, the knocking starts.
Three knocks, a pause, three more.
This time, someone knocks back from the other side of the roof hatch.
You look at Mina.
Mina looks at you.
You finally say it out loud: there is somebody in the freezer.
Why do the dead go still at night?
Because the cold slows them down.
Why do they stay still in the freezer?
Because Rhea went in there on night one.
She was bitten at the fire exit.
She locked herself in the one place that would keep her human.
The envelope was not a map for escaping.
It was a map to reach her.
Then you prepare for the suits.
You cannot stop three people.
But you know what can.
Thirty alarm clocks from aisle 9, and the horn on the van.
Winding them takes one person thirty minutes.
Two people can do it in fifteen.
You are starting to see the point of other people.
At four, the suits cut the shutter.
You drop the bucket one last time, straight into the lot.
Thirty clocks, all set for 4:10.
It is the loudest thing this city has heard in a month.
Every dead thing for a mile turns toward it.
The suits do the smart thing.
They drop their tools and run.
The noise goes with them.
So does the crowd.
By sunrise, the lot is empty.
Day 28.
You open the walk-in freezer.
Frost pours out across the floor.
Rhea sits against the back wall, pale, alive, her eyes open.
How long, she whispers.
You tell her.
She looks past you at the dark store, and the intercom crackles above you.
Attention shoppers, says Rhea's own voice, recorded on night one.
Do not turn the power back on.
Outside, the sun is rising.
The temperature is rising with it.
